paras: The torture of Joe Harris was a series of extralegal attacks in 1880 and 1881 on a prisoner at Rogersville, Hawkins County, Tennessee, accused of the Marble Hall double murder, including a hanging in which the rope broke. Crowds sought to lynch Harris after his arrest, but the sheriff persuaded them to let the law take its course, and Harris was later tried, convicted and legally hanged near Rogersville on November 25, 1881. A Bristol dispatch reported that the torture drew no public censure, which it attributed to local feeling over the murders.

Charles Brown and Andy Heck were killed with an ax at Marble Hall, a large house near Rogersville, their bed set on fire and Brown's pocketbook taken. Sheriff Bob Blevins arrested Harris, a 25-year-old laborer, with Brown's pocketbook on him. He claimed that an unknown man had handed him the pocketbook at the gate, a story the papers did not credit.

According to the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, Harris told his story "when a rope was put around his neck," and it was expected that "short work would be made" of him. The Bristol News reported that when Harris was brought back to Marble Hall, the crowd asked Blevins to hand him over while others prepared fuel "to roast him as he had roasted Brown and Heck." Blevins dissuaded the men, who were his friends, and locked Harris in an iron cage in the Rogersville jail. A Knoxville report likewise credited the sheriff with quelling "a strong feeling and suspicions of lynching" on the Wednesday night.

Two months later, a Bristol dispatch dated January 23, 1881, reported that Harris had been tortured "since his first imprisonment" in several attempts to extort a confession. "On one occasion he was hanged and the rope broke, letting him fall," the dispatch said; on regaining consciousness he offered to show where he had hidden Brown's papers. Nothing was found where he indicated, and the dispatch, which named none of the torturers, said little confidence was placed in his statements.

Harris was tried at Rogersville before Judge N. Hacker and, after five days, convicted of first-degree murder; he was sentenced to hang on April 1, 1881, but appealed. The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction in October 1881 and set the execution for November 25. On execution day, as 2,000 to 2,500 people gathered, a scuffle outside the jail left Harris "believing that the crowd were attempting to capture and lynch him." He was hanged in the pine woods a mile southeast of town after confessing in writing and again on the gallows.

Knoxville and Bristol papers carried most of the coverage, treating Harris's guilt as settled and calling him a "villain" and a "fiend," though the Knoxville Daily Chronicle headlined the averted mob "No Lynching----All Quiet." The torture dispatch, printed in Connecticut's Morning Journal and Courier under the headline "Extorting a Confession—Torturing a Murderer to an Acknowledgement of Crime," reported the torture without reproach and concluded that his lynching "would be witnessed without a shudder by the public."

Reporting the verdict, the Bristol News did not mention the torture. The Chicago Tribune ran a Knoxville dispatch on the execution under "Joe Harris, a Butcher of Two Sleeping Victims, Strung Up at Rogersville, Tenn." None of these reports stated Harris's race, though the Bristol News described his skin as "fair" and a later account set "a colored prisoner" in the jail apart from him.

Accounts of Harris's statements differ: the January dispatch reported admissions under torture, the Bristol News said he "made no confession" at trial, and he confessed in writing and on the gallows. The papers also differ on the date of the murders, given as the night of November 22 by the Bristol News and November 23 by the Knoxville Daily Chronicle and the Tribune's dispatch.

reader.title: Torture of Joe Harris
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Crowds sought to take and lynch Harris after his arrest (A1, A2, A4), and while a prisoner he was tortured by unnamed persons, once by hanging until the rope broke (A5); he was not killed by them and was later legally executed (A10).

Harris survived the torture-hanging and the crowd threats (A5, A2) and died by legal execution after trial and appeal (A8, A10); the crowd threats and torture were extralegal and tied to the murder accusation (A4, A6), but those who hanged him are not named or counted (A5).

The torture and rope-breaking hanging appear only in one Bristol dispatch (A5, A6); the crowd threats after the arrest are reported independently by the Knoxville Daily Chronicle and the Bristol News (A1, A2, A4).

framing.detail: The Bristol dispatch headlined 'Extorting a Confession—Torturing a Murderer' reported the torture without reproach and said his lynching would be witnessed 'without a shudder'.
The Knoxville Daily Chronicle headlined 'No Lynching----All Quiet' and credited the sheriff with calming the crowd, while calling Harris 'the hardened wretch'.
The Bristol News called Harris 'The Marble Hall Fiend' and wrote that the people had decided he should die in a manner to terrify evil doers.
The Chicago Tribune carried a Knoxville dispatch on the execution in a four-hanging roundup headed 'Joe Harris, a Butcher of Two Sleeping Victims, Strung Up'.
